Plan this as a Rhylthyme recipe and deliver a live timeline: Thanksgiving for Eight with One Oven for 8 people
Resource limits: one oven, four burners, two cooks, all dishes finish together.
Everything must be finished by 18:00.

Source text (read all of it):
<<<
Thanksgiving for Eight with One Oven

We eat at six o'clock sharp. There is one oven and four burners, and two of you in the kitchen, so the oven schedule decides everything else. The turkey owns the oven for most of the afternoon; the sides go in while it rests, one after another.

The turkey (14 pounds)
Take the turkey out of the refrigerator 40 minutes before you season it so it is not fridge-cold. Heat the oven to 325°F; give it 20 minutes to come up. Pat the bird dry, rub it all over with softened butter, salt and pepper, and tuck halved onions and thyme into the cavity; this takes about twenty minutes. Roast the turkey for 3 hours, until a thermometer in the thigh reads 165°F. Move the turkey to a carving board and let it rest, loosely tented with foil, for 40 minutes before carving. Carving takes about 15 minutes.

Gravy
As soon as the turkey comes out, pour the pan drippings into a saucepan, whisk in flour and cook for 3 minutes, then whisk in stock and simmer the gravy for 10 minutes until it coats a spoon. Keep it warm over the lowest flame until dinner.

Stuffing
Cut a loaf of day-old bread into cubes and spread them on a sheet pan; you can do this first thing. Twenty minutes before the turkey is due out, melt butter in a skillet and cook diced onion and celery for 10 minutes until soft. Toss the bread with the vegetables, sage and two cups of stock and turn it into a buttered dish; 10 minutes. Bake the stuffing at 375°F for 35 minutes the moment the turkey is out; the oven will already be hot.

Green bean casserole
About ten minutes after the turkey comes out, trim two pounds of green beans and blanch them for 4 minutes in salted boiling water, then drain. Make the mushroom sauce: cook sliced mushrooms in butter for 8 minutes, add cream and simmer for 5 minutes. Combine the beans and sauce in a baking dish and scatter fried onions on top; 5 minutes. Bake the casserole for 20 minutes as soon as the stuffing comes out.

Mashed potatoes
When the turkey comes out, peel and quarter four pounds of potatoes, about 15 minutes, cover with cold salted water and boil for 20 minutes until a knife slides in easily. Drain, then mash with warm cream and a stick of butter; give it 10 minutes. Hold the potatoes covered on the back burner until everything else is ready.

Dinner rolls
The rolls only need warming: slide them into the oven for 8 minutes right after the casserole comes out.

Serve
Carry everything to the table together.
>>>

Each step has exactly one duration kind: fixed with `seconds`, variable with minimum, maximum, and default seconds, or indefinite until the cook ends it. A `startTrigger` connects a step to the program clock or another step through triggers such as `programStart`, offsets, dependencies, manual starts, aborts, or compounds. Every `stepId` must be unique across the entire program, and every task used by a step must have a matching resource constraint whose `maxConcurrent` limits simultaneous use. Repeated work is represented once with `replicates`, while `"each"` chains per-instance follow-up work, `"all"` creates a barrier, and `maxInFlight` prevents more repetitions from starting than the downstream holding area can accommodate. Turn 4 of 4 — relationships, then the program.

Take the step list from turn 3 exactly as it stands.

**First, tracks.** Put each step in a track: one track per parallel line of work — per dish, per station, per instrument, per performer, per sample group. Steps in one track run one after another and must not overlap; anything that runs while something else runs belongs in its own track.

**Second, triggers.** Give every step a `startTrigger` from this vocabulary and no other:

- `{"type":"programStart"}` — at t = 0.
- `{"type":"programStartOffset","offsetSeconds":n}` — n seconds after the start; this is how a short track is delayed so it finishes with the others.
- `{"type":"afterStep","stepId":"x"}` — when x ends. Add `"offsetSeconds"` for a gap, `"event":"start"` to hang off x's start instead of its end, `"instances"` when x is replicated.
- `{"type":"afterStepWithBuffer","stepId":"x","bufferSeconds":n}` — n seconds after x ends.
- `{"type":"manual"}` — the person taps to start it: a gate that no clock can predict (guests seated, dough looks right, the surgeon is ready).
- `{"type":"compound","logic":"all"|"any","triggers":[...]}` — wait for all of, or the first of, several triggers.

**Third, refine the question before you answer it.** Within the scope of scheduling these activities for one person to follow, suggest a better version of the question "which activities depend on which, and which can run at the same time?" — one that would expose dependencies this text implies but does not state: things that must cool, rest, preheat, thaw, proof, be held warm, or be ready at the same moment as something else. Write your improved question out, answer it, and revise the triggers accordingly. A step the improved question reveals is added here, marked `"inferred": true`.

2. Otherwise keep the program you just built; `rhylthyme://guide/authoring` is the cheat-sheet and `rhylthyme://examples/*` are complete programs to pattern-match.
3. Express the limits as constraints, not as copied JSON: the `resourceConstraints`, `replicates`, `instances` and `maxInFlight` you confirmed in turn 2.
4. Run validate_program and fix every error it reports.
